searches.note: Every search returned something of use. Four of the thirty two went to the name of Weinbach's Cuvée Sainte Catherine, which stays contested. Five were restricted to a house's own domain (domaineweinbach.com three times, hugel.com twice, once with m.hugel.com beside it) and read as primary through their summaries; a search drawn mostly from trimbach.fr is read the same way. No WebFetch was tried, since earlier runs found trimbach.fr and Wikipedia refused. Fifteen searches of the share are left unspent.

method: The fragment was written with no web search at all, resting on the Codex's library and region records and on the writer's memory; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and dates, the classification years, the sites and soils, the making and its months, the label words and every beat of the story.

Every source the fragment listed (the Codex's own library, region record and question banks, and two reference books, none opened) is replaced by pages a search returned, read: search; marked primary where the result came from the producer's own domain (trimbach.fr, hugel.com, domaineweinbach.com), a producer's own sheet on a merchant's host (Hameau Albert for Deiss), or the certifying body (Biodyvin).

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's own claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's or critic's own site was read as a lead and never cited. Facts the library states stand as the brief allows, except where a search contested them: the library's no oak for Clos Sainte Hune and its saint's day for Cuvée Sainte Catherine are both contested and reported below.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile (the lint refused hectares in one story, rewritten), no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches. The lint's notes left standing: the first label of 1919 (the house's own page, Decanter and Vinous), the oldest vines of Hugel (the house's own words) and its cask (the house's Guinness claim, hedged), and the first Grand Cru of 1975 (the Codex, with a second source).

tested: The founding of 1626: the house's own history page, as the search summarised it, has a Trimbach of Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines received as a burgher of Riquewihr that year, where he became a grower and winemaker; Falstaff says the same: confirmed, and the town of origin added.

The move to Ribeauvillé: 1920 by the house's page and Falstaff, just after the First World War by Wikipedia, which also has the house at Hunawihr from the 1840s (one source, left out): confirmed with its year.

The clos: more than two centuries in the family and a parcel of a little under two hectares by the house's own page and Palm Bay (the size left out as volatile); Muschelkalk and Lettenkohle bedrock under marly limestone by the house, dolomitic limestone by the Ribeauvillé cooperative's sheet and a writer's site: confirmed, and limestone made precise.

The first label: the house's page has the first label found on the estate, identical to the one printed now, dating from the 1919 vintage; Decanter and Palm Bay call 1919 the first vintage released commercially, Vinous the first produced; iDealwine says the 1919 began its career in 1924: the record says the first label dates from the 1919 vintage.

The making: the house's page gives temperature controlled stainless steel, three or four weeks, no malolactic conversion and a spring bottling, and elsewhere old casks or sometimes steel as the vintage and the volume decide; Decanter has six months in large old casks after the steel and five years in the cellars; Vinous has steel throughout and several years; Palm Bay about five years: corrected from no oak at all to steel or old casks, and to some five years.

Rosacker: Grand Cru in 1983 by one reference site only (left out); the Grand Cru not on the label by the house and the Codex: confirmed. The tier of 1975 and the appellation of 1962 are the Codex's own.

The Schlossberg: Palm Bay's page, in the family's words, has 1.6 hectares bought in 2012 and a first vintage in 2014, released in 2017; Decanter reviews it as Grand Cru Schlossberg: confirmed. A Trimbach Grand Cru Geisberg also exists (a 2014 on a merchant's list); the record does not call the Schlossberg the first.

Saint Hune: canonised by Pope Leo X in 1520, patron of washerwomen, who did the washing of her poor neighbours, dying in 679 by most sources (Wikipedia, Catholic Readings); the village named from her legend (French Moments): added as a legend, the seventh century and 1520.

The rules: nobody living named (the family in the results is listed below), no price, no score (critics' marks met in results, none carried), nothing volatile (the parcel's size and the yearly bottles left out), no judging superlative (no Alsace label teaches more plainly became a plain statement), British, no dash; both questions have one key, options of one kind and an explanation naming the nearest wrong option: sound.

changed.was: Riquewihr is where the Trimbach story starts: in 1626, by the house's own account, a Trimbach was received as a citizen of the town, and the family's record in wine begins there; the house later made its home at Ribeauvillé, a few kilometres north. Between the two towns lies Hunawihr, named, as the clos is, for Saint Hune, a local saint of the early Middle Ages. The family has held its parcel on the slope above the village for some two centuries and bottled the wine under the saint's name long before Alsace had a law of crus. The appellation Alsace came in 1962 and the Grand Cru tier in 1975, and the hill around the clos was later classified as Grand Cru Rosacker. Trimbach kept that name off the label: the clos was known as itself, and the house held that a cru is a site, not a maker's promise. It made the wine as it made everything else, dry, taut and without oak, and released it only after years in the cellar. The house's Schlossberg has carried Grand Cru since the 2014 vintage, while Clos Sainte Hune has never done so. No Alsace label teaches more plainly that a parcel's own name can say more than its appellation.
changed.now: Riquewihr is where the Trimbach story starts: in 1626, by the house's own account, a Trimbach from Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines was received as a citizen of the town and took up the vine there. The family moved its house to Ribeauvillé, a few kilometres north, in 1920. Between the two towns lies Hunawihr, named, as the clos is, for Saint Hune, a noblewoman of the seventh century who, the legend goes, washed the clothes of the poor; she was made a saint in 1520. The family has held its parcel above the village for more than two centuries; the first label to bear the clos's name, of a design unchanged since, dates from the 1919 vintage. The appellation Alsace came in 1962 and the Grand Cru tier in 1975, and the hill around the clos was later classified as Grand Cru Rosacker. Trimbach chose to keep that name off the label and sell the wine as Alsace under the clos's own name, dry, with no malolactic conversion, and only after some five years in its cellars. The family bought vines on the Schlossberg in 2012, and that wine has carried the Grand Cru name since the 2014 vintage; Clos Sainte Hune never has. Its label shows plainly that a parcel's own name can say more than its appellation.
changed.why: Sainte-Marie-aux-Mines and 1920 are the house's own (with Falstaff); Saint Hune's legend and 1520 are in two secondary sources; the 1919 label in the house's page and Decanter; the Schlossberg of 2012 and 2014 in the family's words on Palm Bay's page with Decanter's review; the house's view of a cru as a site was the Codex's reading, not the family's words, and is cut; the last sentence no longer ranks the label above all others.

tested: The founding of 1639 in the Thirty Years War: the house's own pages have Riquewihr since 1639; its presentation of 2015 has Hans Ulrich Hugel, a Swiss, settling there that year in the war; Decanter's timeline has him made a freeman of the town that year: confirmed; the founder is described, for want of his dates.

The cask of 1715: named Sainte Catherine and listed by Guinness as the oldest working cask, by the house's own pages, its presentation and Cellar Tours: confirmed as the house's claim; oval was found nowhere and is cut.
Jean Hugel, known as Johnny: 28 September 1924 to 9 June 2009 by Wikipedia, 1924 to 2009 on the house's own page, dead at 84 in 2009 by Decanter: named with his dates.

The law: Wikipedia credits him with first using the words Vendange Tardive for the 1976 wines and drafting the rules accepted by the INAO on 1 March 1984; the house's page says the family drafted the rules and they became law in 1984; Decanter's Wine Legend of the 1976 SGN says the rules were promulgated in 1984 and twice revised: confirmed, and the earlier telling (late harvests sold under those names through the twentieth century, a campaign of growers) corrected.
The minimums: Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris above Riesling and Muscat by Wikipedia and the Codex's Alsace record: confirmed.

The sites: the house's own sheets for the wine have its Vendange Tardive from the oldest parcels of the estate within the Sporen, on Lias clay and marl decalcified at the surface; Frederick Wildman has the family's Sporen parcel on clay and chalk: confirmed and made precise.

The making: the house's sheets give a few hours of settling, temperature controlled casks or vats at 18 to 24 degrees, one racking before winter, a natural clearing, a light filtration and a spring bottling; Frederick Wildman has a cold ferment and neutral vessels; Decanter's note lists it as unoaked: the large old oak casks and the yeast stopping of its own accord are corrected.

The ageing and service: the house gives fifteen to twenty years for the 2010 and eight to twelve for the 2006, and 8 degrees for the 2010: the record's ten to twenty years and 6 to 8 degrees stand. Its Gewurztraminer Sélection de Grains Nobles was not made in 1990, a year without noble rot, by the house's sheet: added.

The rules: nobody living named (the family in the results is listed below), no price, no score, nothing volatile (the hectares in the results left out), no judging superlative (the Guinness claim is the house's, hedged; oldest vines are the house's own words), British, no dash; both questions sound.

changed.was: The Thirty Years War had not yet ended when the Hugels came to Riquewihr in 1639, by the family's own account, and they have made wine inside its walls ever since. Their cellar keeps a great oval cask, the Sainte Catherine, made in 1715 and, as the house tells it, in use ever since. In the ripe autumns of the twentieth century the family picked overripe and noble rot grapes in separate late passes and sold them as Vendange Tardive and Sélection de Grains Nobles, words that then had no legal meaning. After the rich vintage of 1976 a son of the house led the growers' campaign for rules, and in 1984 French law defined both terms: the four noble grapes alone, a minimum sugar for each, the picking declared in advance and checked, and no sugar added. Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris must reach a higher minimum than Riesling and Muscat. Hugel long left the names of its Grand Cru slopes off its labels, so its late harvest wines speak of Riquewihr and the year rather than of a cru. When the 2021 vintage brought a compulsory sweetness mention to Alsace whites, the two late harvest terms were spared it, since each already tells the guest what the bottle holds. Every bottle is the law of 1984 at work, late picked with nothing added, its sweetness the grape's own.
changed.now: The Thirty Years War had not yet ended when a Swiss-born Hugel settled at Riquewihr in 1639, by the family's own account, and was made a freeman of the town; his descendants have made wine there ever since. Their cellar keeps a cask of 1715, the Sainte Catherine, which the house says Guinness has recognised as the oldest working cask in the world. After the hot summer of 1976, Jean Hugel (1924 to 2009), known as Johnny, is credited with first putting the words Vendange Tardive on late picked wines, words that then had no meaning in law, and he drafted rules to give them one. In 1984 French law defined both late harvest terms: the four noble grapes alone, a minimum sugar for each, the picking declared in advance and checked, and no sugar added. Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris must reach a higher minimum than Riesling and Muscat. Hugel long left its Grand Cru names off its labels, so its late harvest Gewurztraminer speaks of Riquewihr and the year, though it grows in the Sporen. When the 2021 vintage brought a compulsory sweetness mention to Alsace whites, the two late harvest terms were spared it. Every bottle is the law of 1984 at work: late picked, nothing added, its sweetness the grape's own.
changed.why: The Swiss founder made a freeman in 1639 by the house and Decanter; the cask as the house's Guinness claim; Jean Hugel's dates by the house, Wikipedia and Decanter; first using the words for the 1976 wines by Wikipedia; the rules drafted and made law in 1984 by the house and Decanter; the Sporen by the house's sheets.

changed.was: Two families' vines became one domaine in 1959, when a Humbrecht grower, from a family that had tended vines south of Colmar since the seventeenth century by its own account, married a daughter of the Zind family, and the domaine took both names. In 1977 the family bought Clos Saint Urbain, a parcel of the Rangen above Thann whose steepness had left much of the hill neglected; few growers then wished to work rock so hard to farm. The Rangen was classified Grand Cru in 1983, and the clos became the domaine's southernmost wine, far from its home at Turckheim. In 1989 the founders' son became the first French winemaker to pass the Master of Wine examination. He took the domaine to very low yields, slow ferments with the grapes' own yeasts in old casks and, from the late 1990s, biodynamic farming. Because those ferments often stopped short of dryness, the domaine began printing its own sweetness index on the label, years before Alsace law made a sweetness mention compulsory with the 2021 vintage. Clos Saint Urbain puts the Rangen in one bottle: volcanic rock, a hand worked slope and a label that warns the guest how sweet the glass will be.
changed.now: Two families' vines became one domaine in 1959, when a Humbrecht grower of Gueberschwihr, from a family that had tended vines there since 1620 by its own account, married a daughter of the Zind family of Wintzenheim, and the domaine took both names. Far to the south, above Thann, the Rangen had almost fallen out of use: by the end of the 1960s phylloxera, two world wars and the toil of its slopes had left only a small part of the hill in vine. In 1977 the family bought Clos Saint Urbain there, named for the chapel among its vines, and replanted the neglected slope. The Rangen was classified Grand Cru in 1983, and in 1989 the founders' son became France's first Master of Wine. The domaine came to be known for very low yields, slow ferments with the grapes' own yeasts in old casks and, from 1997, biodynamic farming, certified in 2002. With so many of those ferments stopping short of dryness, it began printing its own sweetness index, from 1 to 5, on its labels, years before Alsace law made a sweetness mention compulsory with the 2021 vintage. Clos Saint Urbain puts the Rangen in one bottle: volcanic rock, a hand worked slope and a label that warns the guest how sweet the glass will be.
changed.why: Gueberschwihr, Wintzenheim and 1620 by Wikipedia, iDealwine and Alliance Wine; the Rangen's decline and replanting by The World of Fine Wine and Vinous; 1977 and 1983 by The World of Fine Wine with Vinous and FRW; France's first Master of Wine by Decanter and Wikipedia; biodynamic from 1997 and certified in 2002 by Kobrand, Alliance Wine and Biodyvin; the index from 1 to 5 by Wikipedia and Decanter; the son no longer credited with the domaine's methods, which no source gave to him.

The death of 1979 and the widow and two daughters who carried the domaine on: the domaine's magazine of 2013 to 2014 and Decanter's obituary of the widow: confirmed; for more than three decades was not searched and is cut.
The Schlossberg first Grand Cru in 1975 on granite: the Codex, with a reference site that dates the tier from 1975 for the Schlossberg: stands.

Cuvée Sainte Catherine: four searches. The library says it is named for Saint Catherine's day and made from later picked fruit; one merchant says it takes its name from the saint's day, 25 November, when the first vintages were picked; another merchant and the domaine's own page, as the search summarised it, name the cuvée after a member of the Faller family; the domaine places it on the lower part of the slope, from very old vines, fuller and richer than its other Schlossberg Rieslings; one merchant places it mid slope; another says picked later than average. The making: the domaine's own page on its cellar gives gentle, gradual pressing and long ferments with indigenous yeasts alone in old oak foudres: confirmed; the lees until bottling found nowhere and cut.
The label: Clos des Capucins with the cuvée and the Grand Cru on a merchant's listing, and the Codex's own question on the labels bearing the Clos des Capucins: confirmed.

changed.was: In 1612, as the domaine tells it, Capuchin friars planted the walled vineyard below the Schlossberg, and the little stream that runs through it, the Weinbach, later gave the estate its name. The Revolution took the friars' clos and sold it as national property, and in 1898 the Faller family bought it. The granite hill above became the first Grand Cru of Alsace in 1975. After the death of the head of the family in 1979, his widow and their two daughters ran the domaine for more than three decades, and they built its name for ripe, perfumed wines called after the family and the saints rather than after sites: Cuvée Théo for the late husband, Cuvée Laurence, and Sainte Catherine for the saint's day in late November, when the last grapes came in. The vineyards came to be farmed biodynamically, and the women of the family made the domaine a house that a guest knows by its first names. Hence the rule its labels teach, that in Alsace a cuvée may honour a person or a saint while only the cru tells you where the grapes grew.
changed.now: The walled vineyard below the Schlossberg is recorded as early as 890, and in 1612, as the domaine tells it, Capuchin friars built their house there; the little stream that runs through it, the Weinbach, or wine stream, later gave the estate its name. The Revolution took the friars' clos and sold it as national property, and in 1898 two Faller brothers bought it and passed it on to the next generation of the family. The granite hill above became the first Grand Cru of Alsace in 1975. After the head of the family died in 1979, his widow and their two daughters carried the domaine on, and they built its name for ripe, perfumed wines called after the family rather than after sites: Cuvée Théo for the late husband, Cuvée Laurence and Cuvée Sainte Catherine, an old vine selection from the lower slope of the Schlossberg. Each cuvée is a selection of parcels within a site, fermented with its own yeasts in old foudres. The vineyards came to be farmed biodynamically, and the women of the family made the domaine a house that a guest knows by its first names. Hence the rule its labels teach, that in Alsace a cuvée may honour a person while only the cru tells you where the grapes grew.
changed.why: The clos of 890, the friars' house of 1612, the wine stream, the Revolution's sale, the brothers of 1898, the death of 1979 and the widow and daughters, the cuvées as parcel selections and the foudres with native yeasts are all the domaine's own account, with Grand Cru Wijnen, Regal and Decanter beside it; the saint's day and the last grapes of late November are cut as contested, and the three decades as unsearched.

changed.was: The founder whose name the domaine carries came home to Bergheim after the Second World War and set up the domaine in 1947, selling wine by grape, as Alsace did. His grandson took charge in the 1970s and came to argue that the grape was hiding the place: the old vineyards of Alsace, he held, had been planted with many varieties together, and the great hills were known by name long before anyone sold their wine by grape. He replanted parcels with mixed varieties, farmed them biodynamically and labelled them by site alone, at first against the rules, which asked a Grand Cru for a single noble grape. The argument won ground. The rules of the Altenberg de Bergheim were rewritten to admit a blend of the hill, and Kaefferkopf, admitted in 2007 as the fifty-first Grand Cru, took blends as well. When each Grand Cru became an appellation of its own in 2011, the Altenberg kept that right in its own rules. The domaine bottles the Altenberg, the Schoenenbourg and the Mambourg as field blends, each named for its hill. The Altenberg answers an old Alsace question: a Grand Cru may name its place and no grape at all.

In the 2000s the rules of the Altenberg de Bergheim were rewritten to admit a blend of the hill, and Kaefferkopf, admitted in 2007 as the fifty-first Grand Cru, took blends as well. When each Grand Cru became an appellation of its own in 2011, the Altenberg kept that right in its own rules. The domaine bottles the Altenberg, the Schoenenbourg and the Mambourg as field blends, each named for its hill. picks.ruling: kept: Clos Sainte Hune is the house's flagship by every source, a family parcel since before the house's own first label of 1919.

kept: the Gewurztraminer Vendange Tardive comes from the house's oldest Sporen vines by its own sheets and carries the law the family drafted; the house also makes the Riesling and Pinot Gris late harvests, which the record does not need.
kept: the Riesling of Clos Saint Urbain on the Rangen, the domaine's monopole, bought in 1977.

kept, with a note for the integrator: Cuvée Sainte Catherine is the domaine's Schlossberg flagship, but the origin of its name is contested (the saint's day by the library and one merchant, a member of the family by the domaine's page as summarised), so the record teaches it only as a house name for old vines on the lower slope.
kept: the Altenberg de Bergheim is the field blend the domaine is known for; the label prints Altenberg de Bergheim Grand Cru, which holds the plan's words.

codexInTension.says: Clos Ste Hune fermented dry in stainless steel with no oak; the house style stainless steel.
codexInTension.against: The house's own page has the clos made in old casks or sometimes in stainless steel as the vintage and the volume decide (and elsewhere steel); Decanter has about six months in large old casks after the steel. No new oak holds; no oak at all does not.
